extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, philosophy of language, and science (authors who must craft or evaluate definitions and classifications)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on what a correct or useful definition is, how definitions relate to classification and scientific practice, and how to distinguish essential from accidental predicates. Covers when definitions can serve as premises and when covert factual postulates are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proprium (attribute necessarily following connotation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Proprium of the species is any attribute which belongs to all the individuals included in the species and which, though not connoted by the specific name, yet follows from some attribute which the name either ordinarily or specially connotes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two kinds: (a) Proprium of the first kind follows by demonstration (e.g., opposite sides equal follows from a parallelogram's connoted attributes); (b) Proprium of the second kind follows by causation (e.g., ability to understand language follows from rationality in man). In both cases the following is necessary — its not following would be inconsistent with some law regarded as part of our thinking faculty or the universe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accidens (attributes not connoted nor necessarily connected)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accidens includes all attributes which are neither involved in the signification of the name nor have, so far as we know, any necessary connection with attributes which are so involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divided into inseparable accidents (universal to the species but not necessary — e.g., blackness of crows as known now) and separable accidents (sometimes absent, or only present at some times — e.g., color of a European, being born). Do not treat accidental attributes as part of a term's connotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition as declaration of meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: The simplest and most correct notion of a definition is a proposition declaratory of the meaning of a word — either its common acceptation or the meaning the speaker/writer intends to annex for particular purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper names (mere marks for individuals) cannot be defined. Connotative names should be defined by stating their connotation directly (explicit list of attributes) or indirectly by predicate names that together connote the same aggregation of attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete (philosophical) definition = full connotation/analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition of a name, according to this view, is the sum total of all the essential propositions which can be framed with that name for their subject — all propositions whose truth is implied in the name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A complete definition allows evolving every proposition implied in the name without other premises; equivalently, definition is an analysis of the complex whole into its constituent attributes. Brevity is secondary to completeness for philosophical definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of abstract names by analyzing foundational phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: When an abstract name denotes a single attribute, its definition must be sought in the fact or phenomenon (the foundation of the attribute) from which it derives its meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze the phenomenon into constituent parts (co-existent or successive). Example: eloquence defined as the power of influencing the feelings by speech or writing — obtained by resolving the causal phenomenon into cause and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple sensations often indefinable verbally
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of simple feelings or states of consciousness are, in general, unsusceptible of definition by other words because their meaning rests on individual experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such names are analogous to proper names: their signification can only be conveyed by appeal to personal experience (e.g., 'sensation of white').

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential-but-incomplete definitions (per genus et differentiam practised)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defining a connotative term by a part only of its connotation (e.g., 'Man is a rational animal') can serve as a sufficient definition for ordinary purposes if the stated attributes suffice to mark out the current denotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These definitions are practically useful and common (the classical 'per genus et differentiam'), but they are vulnerable to being overturned by discovery of new objects that share the stated attributes but differ in omitted ones (e.g., hypothetical Houyhnhnms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accidental definitions (descriptions) are not genuine definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Defining a class by any of its accidents — attributes not included in its connotation — is a description, not a genuine definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A description can function as a discriminator if it is convertible with the name (co-extensive), but it does not state the essence. Such descriptions may be elevated to genuine definitions when a special or technical connotation is intentionally attached to a term for classification purposes (e.g., scientific definitions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Convertibility/co-extensionality test for acceptable descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: A definition or description is correct if it is convertible with the name it professes to define — i.e., predicable of every thing of which the name is predicable and of nothing else.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the practical test that can make an otherwise accidental description acceptable as a working definition, but convertibility does not guarantee that the definition expresses the original connotation or essence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific/technical definitions serve classification and are provisional
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific definitions typically assign a special connotation to a general name to suit a system of classification; they serve as landmarks of classification rather than as immutable analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific definitions change as knowledge advances (example: the connotation of 'acid' changed with chemical discoveries). Accept that scientific definitions are progressive and provisional and should be chosen to fit the classificatory purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition must include traits sufficient to fix class boundaries
rubrics_metrics.description: A useful definition must connote enough properties to fix the boundaries of the class — to indicate what kinds include it or are included by it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As long as the definition fully states the connotation needed to mark class boundaries, it accomplishes what a definition can be required to do. Enumerating all connoted properties ensures that the place of the class in a taxonomy is clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of per genus et differentiam (highest genus problem)
rubrics_metrics.description: The classical rule that every definition must be per genus et differentiam is not universally tenable: the highest or summum genus has no superior genus to be used in such a definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If genus-and-differentia is used, 'differentia' should represent all peculiarities constitutive of the species (plural differentiae), but recognize that some names (e.g., those of simple feelings or highest genera) cannot be fully treated by this formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish definitions of names from covert postulates about things
rubrics_metrics.description: All definitions are of names (nominal); propositions that purport to be 'definitions of things' in fact combine a nominal definition with a covert assertion (postulate) that things corresponding to the definition exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the two distinct components when a definition seems to assert existence: (1) the nominal definition (meaning), which is neither true nor false but conformable to usage; (2) the covert factual postulate (existence/possibility), which is truth-evaluable and serves as a premise for further reasoning (e.g., Euclid's circle contains both).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions alone are not factual premises; require explicit postulates for existence
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrations that rely on what appear to be definitions actually depend on the tacit postulates that objects with the defined properties may exist; the definition (meaning) itself supplies only linguistic relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use a bare definition as a factual premise from which to infer physical consequences. Make any existence or possibility assumptions explicit as postulates (Euclid example: 'a figure may exist with all points equidistant from a centre').

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid drawing empirical conclusions solely from definitional premises
rubrics_metrics.description: If a definition's nominal form is used as a premise without the postulate of real existence, one may derive false empirical conclusions (illustrated by the dragon syllogism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substitute 'means' for 'is' to check whether conclusions follow purely from meanings or also require assumptions of existence. Ensure that syllogisms intended to reach factual conclusions include premises asserting existence where needed.
